summary:
We designed and built New Horizon, a web app that finds the places on Earth that look most like a chosen site on Mars. Users pick one of five Mars sites: the Jezero crater rim, Bradbury Landing in Gale crater, Victoria Crater, Nili Patera and Athabasca Valles. The app then compares the site near 18 thousand bare desert, mountain and polar locations on Earth.

The comparison uses real NASA and ESA satellite data. For each 10 × 10 km area we measure slope, height differences and roughness the same way on both planets. Optional sliders include wind speed and surface brightness. Users choose which properties matter most, and the app shows the ten best Earth matches on a map with a clear score. It also shows charts, context such as geology and thermal inertia, and honest notes on what cannot be compared, such as soil strength and air pressure.

This matters because equipment must be tested on Earth before it goes to Mars. Choosing a test site is usually slow and based on experience. Our tool makes the choice fast, open and based on data, so teams can find the right test terrain for their mission.
details:
New Horizon is a web app that finds the places on Earth that are most similar to a chosen site on Mars. Teams can use these places to test rovers, instruments and procedures before a mission.

How it works: The user picks one of five Mars sites: Jezero crater rim, Bradbury Landing in Gale crater, Victoria Crater, Nili Patera or Athabasca Valles. For each site we measured the terrain of a 10 × 10 km area from orbital elevation data (MOLA, CTX and HRSC): median slope, local relief (the height difference between low and high ground) and roughness. We then measured the same features, with exactly the same code, for 17,735 bare desert, mountain and polar locations on Earth, using the Copernicus 30 m elevation model. These locations were selected from 25,467 candidates with MODIS vegetation and land-cover data. The app compares the numbers with a transparent weighted formula and shows the ten closest Earth matches on a map, each at least 50 km apart. Sliders let users decide what matters most for their mission, and optional sliders add wind speed (MACDA and MERRA-2) and surface brightness (OMEGA and MODIS).

Benefits and impact: Choosing a Mars test site is usually based on experience and reputation. New Horizon makes it fast, open and data-driven, so any team, from space agencies to students, can find the right practice terrain for its own target on Mars. In the future it could support landing-site planning, astronaut training and Moon analogs for Artemis.

Tools: Python (NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, xarray) for data processing, Google Earth Engine for satellite data, and JavaScript with React, Vite, Leaflet and Recharts for the website. We used GitHub for teamwork and Netlify for hosting.

Creativity: The same terrain fingerprint runs on two planets, and the app searches the whole Earth instead of a short list of famous sites. It is also honest by design: every match shows what matches, what differs and what cannot be compared.

Factors we considered: using identical methods and resolution (about 455 m) on both planets; filtering out vegetated, urban, water and snow areas; verifying every data source; making the score easy to understand (it is not a "% Mars-like" value); and clearly showing limits, such as soil strength, rock size and air pressure, which our data cannot compare.
